D1:
Why: Core is the lowest AnimationPriority, the same level the default Animate script's idle/walk use at Idle/Movement and below. When tracks of different priority animate the same joints, the higher priority wins, so the Idle/Movement animations override the Core swing on the arms. Also Humanoid:LoadAnimation is deprecated, and loading a new track every click leaks tracks.
Fix: set the priority to Action (or Action2-4) and re-publish, or set it in code. Load once through the Animator:
```lua
local char = player.Character or player.CharacterAdded:Wait()
local animator = char:WaitForChild("Humanoid"):WaitForChild("Animator")
local track = animator:LoadAnimation(script.SwingAnim)
track.Priority = Enum.AnimationPriority.Action
tool.Activated:Connect(function()
    if not track.IsPlaying then track:Play() end
end)
```
Reload the track on CharacterAdded, because the old Animator is destroyed on respawn.
D2:
1) Server Script: each client owns its own camera. workspace.CurrentCamera on the server is not the player's camera and does not replicate, so nothing happens. Camera code must run in a LocalScript.
2) LocalScript: Camera.CameraType is still Custom, so the default PlayerModule camera controller rewrites CFrame every frame to follow the character, and it snaps back. The script may also run before the camera or CutsceneCam exists.
Fix:
```lua
local cam = workspace.CurrentCamera
local target = workspace:WaitForChild("CutsceneCam")
cam.CameraType = Enum.CameraType.Scriptable
cam.CFrame = target.CFrame -- or TweenService for a moving shot
-- when the cutscene ends:
-- cam.CameraType = Enum.CameraType.Custom
-- cam.CameraSubject = player.Character:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
```
Some setups reset the camera after spawn, so if needed set it after a task.wait()/RenderStepped or on CurrentCamera changes. Restore Custom afterwards.
D3:
The fixed CanvasSize of 600 offset pixels does not grow with the content. With 40 items the list is taller than 600 px, so anything past that can't be scrolled to. With 8 items there is empty scroll space.
Cleanest fix: set ScrollingFrame.AutomaticCanvasSize = Enum.AutomaticSize.Y and CanvasSize = UDim2.new(0,0,0,0), and let the engine size the canvas from the content. Alternative: update from the layout, e.g. `list:GetPropertyChangedSignal("AbsoluteContentSize"):Connect(function() sf.CanvasSize = UDim2.fromOffset(0, list.AbsoluteContentSize.Y + padding) end)`.
Also: give the items a fixed offset height (or a UIAspectRatioConstraint), not a Y scale relative to the canvas, because scale-Y children and automatic canvas feed back into each other. Account for UIPadding, and set ScrollingDirection = Y.
D4:
1) Too weak: a 20x2x20 part of default Plastic (density 0.7) has mass 560. Weight is mass x workspace.Gravity (196.2), about 110,000 force units, so 5000 is far below it. Compute the force: Force = Vector3.new(0, part.AssemblyMass * workspace.Gravity, 0), plus a margin to climb. Better still, use AlignPosition or a PD controller for a stable hover height.
2) Off-centre attachment: the force acts at the corner, so it creates torque. As the part tilts, the force (RelativeTo defaults to Attachment0, the part's local frame) tilts with it and gains a sideways component, so the part slides and spins away.
Fix: put Attachment0 at the centre of mass (Position 0,0,0 for one part), set VectorForce.RelativeTo = Enum.ActuatorRelativeTo.World so the force always points up, and set ApplyAtCenterOfMass = true. Add an AlignOrientation (or AngularVelocity with MaxTorque) to keep it level, and set server network ownership if the server drives it.
D5:
Leaks:
1) sessions[player] is never removed. The table holds strong refs to Player objects and their growing history tables.
2) Each CharacterAdded makes a new Heartbeat connection that is never disconnected. After every respawn the old connections keep running on dead characters (and keep them in memory), so N respawns means N updaters per player.
3) The CharacterAdded connection itself, and the history tables if they grow without a cap.
Fix:
```lua
local conns = {}
Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(player)
    sessions[player] = { kills = 0, history = {} }
    player.CharacterAdded:Connect(function(char)
        if conns[player] then conns[player]:Disconnect() end
        conns[player] = RunService.Heartbeat:Connect(function()
            if char.Parent then updateAura(char) end
        end)
        char.Destroying:Connect(function() -- or Humanoid.Died
            if conns[player] then conns[player]:Disconnect(); conns[player] = nil end
        end)
    end)
end)
Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(player)
    if conns[player] then conns[player]:Disconnect(); conns[player] = nil end
    sessions[player] = nil
end)
```
Better: run one Heartbeat loop that iterates the active characters instead of one per player. Cap history (a ring buffer), set workspace.PlayerCharacterDestroyBehavior to Enabled, and check memory with the Dev Console Memory/LuaHeap view.

```lua
local function attachPet(pet: BasePart, player: Player)
    local hrp = player.Character:WaitForChild("HumanoidRootPart")
    pet.Anchored = false; pet.CanCollide = false; pet.Massless = true
    local a0 = Instance.new("Attachment", pet)
    local a1 = Instance.new("Attachment", hrp)
    a1.Position = Vector3.new(0, 2, 3) -- +Z is behind (LookVector is -Z)
    local ap = Instance.new("AlignPosition")
    ap.Attachment0, ap.Attachment1 = a0, a1
    ap.Responsiveness = 15; ap.MaxForce = 1e5; ap.Parent = pet
    local ao = Instance.new("AlignOrientation")
    ao.Attachment0, ao.Attachment1 = a0, a1
    ao.Responsiveness = 15; ao.MaxTorque = 1e5; ao.Parent = pet
    pet.Parent = player.Character
    pet:SetNetworkOwner(player)
end
```
Key rules: use AlignPosition/AlignOrientation (two-attachment mode) with Responsiveness for smoothing. Don't weld the pet or set CFrame every frame. Make the pet Massless and non-colliding so it doesn't push the player. The offset is in HRP local space. Give network ownership to the owner (or keep the server and accept latency). Never anchor it. Clean up on CharacterRemoving/respawn, and destroy the attachments.
D7:
```lua
local PFS = game:GetService("PathfindingService")
local path = PFS:CreatePath({
    AgentRadius = 2, AgentHeight = 5, AgentCanJump = true,
    Costs = { Lava = math.huge, Water = 20 },
})
local function moveTo(humanoid: Humanoid, goal: Vector3)
    local root = humanoid.RootPart
    local ok = pcall(path.ComputeAsync, path, root.Position, goal)
    if not ok or path.Status ~= Enum.PathStatus.Success then return false end
    for _, wp in path:GetWaypoints() do
        if wp.Action == Enum.PathWaypointAction.Jump then humanoid.Jump = true end
        humanoid:MoveTo(wp.Position)
        if not humanoid.MoveToFinished:Wait() then return false end
    end
    return true
end
```
Key rules: a cost of math.huge makes a PathfindingModifier label (or material) impassable. Water is a terrain material name, and a moderate cost means it is avoided but used if there is no reasonable dry route. The modifier's Label must match the Costs key exactly. Wrap ComputeAsync in pcall and check Status. Handle Jump waypoints. MoveTo times out after 8 s, so loop per waypoint. Listen to path.Blocked and recompute. Set root:SetNetworkOwner(nil) for smooth server NPCs.

local DSS = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local wins = DSS:GetOrderedDataStore("Wins")
local function refresh(board)
    local ok, pages = pcall(wins.GetSortedAsync, wins, false, 10) -- descending, top 10

Write with IncrementAsync or SetAsync when wins change, not every frame. pcall every call and refresh about every 60 s or more, because GetSortedAsync has its own request budget. ```lua
local SoundService = game:GetService("SoundService")
SoundService.DefaultListenerLocation = Enum.ListenerLocation.Camera -- auto listener -> output
local function wire(src, dst)
    local w = Instance.new("Wire"); w.SourceInstance = src; w.TargetInstance = dst; w.Parent = dst
end
-- (a) non-spatial music: Player -> DeviceOutput directly
local music = Instance.new("AudioPlayer")
music.Asset = "rbxassetid://MUSIC_ID"; music.Looping = true; music.Parent = SoundService
local out = Instance.new("AudioDeviceOutput"); out.Parent = SoundService
wire(music, out)
music:Play()
-- (b) spatial campfire: Player -> Emitter on the part
local crackle = Instance.new("AudioPlayer")
crackle.Asset = "rbxassetid://FIRE_ID"; crackle.Looping = true; crackle.Parent = campfire
local emitter = Instance.new("AudioEmitter"); emitter.Parent = campfire
emitter.DistanceAttenuationMode = Enum.DistanceAttenuationMode.InverseTapered -- or SetDistanceAttenuation({[0]=1,[10]=0.6,[60]=0})
wire(crackle, emitter)
crackle:Play()
```
Key rules: nothing plays unless it is wired. Spatial = AudioPlayer to AudioEmitter (parented to the part), heard by an AudioListener wired to AudioDeviceOutput (or set DefaultListenerLocation to Character/Camera). Non-spatial = wire straight to the output. Use InverseTapered or a custom curve so it fades with no hard cut. Emitter and listener must share an AudioInteractionGroup. Assets must be allowed for the experience.

D11:
Cars: give the driver network ownership of the whole vehicle assembly (VehicleSeat does this automatically when a player sits, or call SetNetworkOwner(driver) on the chassis root on the server when the Occupant changes). The driver then simulates locally with no input lag. Return it to the server (SetNetworkOwner(nil)) or auto when they leave. Never anchor parts mid-drive, because anchored parts are always server-owned.
NPC guards: SetNetworkOwner(nil) on the HumanoidRootPart (or every part) after spawning, so ownership never ping-pongs to nearby players. That stops jitter, and players can't move them.
Security: whoever owns an assembly is trusted for its physics. Exploiters can teleport or fling anything they own, including their car and anything it touches. Physics contacts between client-owned and server parts can still be abused, so the server must validate car speed and position deltas, distances, and damage or kill events, not trust them. With auto ownership a guard can end up owned by an exploiter, which is why guards are server-owned. For a competitive game consider Workspace.AuthorityMode = Server (2026 Server Authority), which makes the server authoritative with client prediction instead of trusting owners.
D12:
What the engine keeps: standard DataStores version every write automatically. Superseded versions are kept for 30 days, at most about one backup per key per UTC hour. Ordered DataStores have no versions.
APIs: DataStore:ListVersionsAsync(key, Enum.SortDirection, minDate, maxDate, pageSize) to browse versions, GetVersionAsync(key, version) to read one, and the simpler GetVersionAtTimeAsync(key, timestampMs) to get the version current at a time (just before the update). Open Cloud DataStore v2 endpoints offer the same for an external tool.
Tool flow: an admin enters a UserId and the update time. Load that version and show a diff. Make sure the player is offline or kick them, and respect the session lock. Write with UpdateAsync (with a backup or audit log of the current value) and mark the profile restored, so live autosave doesn't overwrite it.
Limits: the 30-day window, hourly granularity (a write within the same hour as the bad update can be lost, along with progress made after it), the normal per-key and experience request budgets (4 MB/min write per key, etc.), the 4 MB value limit, and keys that were removed by RemoveAsync but are still retrievable inside 30 days. Restoring also rolls back legitimate progress and purchases made since, so reconcile purchase receipts.
D13:
Architecture: web panel, then your backend (auth, audit log, admin roles), then Roblox Open Cloud using an API key with minimal scope restricted to this universe, kept in the backend's secret manager and never in the browser.
(1) Announcements: the backend calls Open Cloud Messaging (POST cloud/v2/universes/{id}:publishMessage, topic "Announce", payload under 1 KB). Every live server does MessagingService:SubscribeAsync("Announce", ...) at startup, then validates the payload and fires the clients. Delivery is best effort and arrives within seconds. Also store the latest announcement in a DataStore or MemoryStore so new servers pick it up.
(2) Item grant: don't edit the profile directly while the player may be in a session (the live session would overwrite it). Write a grant record to a "PendingGrants" store via Open Cloud DataStore/MemoryStore (key = UserId, list of {grantId, item}). Publish a "grant" message so the server holding the player claims it immediately. Otherwise the server claims it on join: UpdateAsync the profile, apply only grantIds not already applied (idempotent), then delete the pending entry. Log everything.
Limits: Open Cloud writes share the experience's DataStore budget, the API key permissions, and MessagingService rate and 1 KB limits.
D14:
BindableEvents (like remotes) copy arguments across the boundary. Tables are deep-copied, and metatables are stripped, so invObject arrives as a plain table: method calls (obj:Add()) are nil, and mutations hit a copy, not the original state. Other limits: mixed or non-string keys are lost or converted, functions are dropped, and Instances are passed by reference (the player is fine). Each Fire also has cross-script overhead and deferred ordering.
ModuleScripts: require() returns the same table to every Script in the same VM context (cached per environment), so the scripts share real references. Make an InventoryService module that owns the state (inventories[player]) and exposes functions or class objects. Other server modules require it and call methods directly, with metatables intact and no copying. Keep one entry Script that requires the services (a single-script architecture), use plain function calls or module-level signals for events, and keep BindableEvents only for loose decoupling with plain data (ids, numbers), never live objects.
D15:
Use UnreliableRemoteEvent for high-frequency, cosmetic, superseded-by-the-next-update data: aim direction, look angles, footstep and cosmetic VFX triggers, and continuous positions. Losing or reordering one packet is fine because the next one replaces it. It doesn't occupy the reliable ordered queue, so hits and purchases stay on normal RemoteEvents and no longer wait behind aim spam.
Constraints: delivery is best effort with no ordering or delivery guarantee, so include a sequence number or timestamp and drop stale ones. The payload limit is about 1000 bytes, and larger payloads are dropped, so send compact data (quantized angles, ids). Messages over the rate limit are dropped, not queued. Messages with no listener connected are discarded. It is still client input, so validate and rate-limit it on the server.
Also reduce the volume: send at 10-20 Hz only when the value changes, batch per tick, and on the server re-broadcast only to nearby clients (FireClient to relevant players) rather than FireAllClients. Never use it for purchases, damage, inventory or state changes.
D16:
- Message size limit is 1 KB, so a ~3 KB JSON payload fails outright.
- Every subscriber receives every message on a topic. 500 servers each publishing every 5 s is 6000 messages per minute, delivered to all 500 servers, about 3 million receives per minute. The per-topic receive limit is roughly 40 + 80 x servers per minute (about 40k) and the experience-wide limit is 400 + 200 x servers per minute, so it throttles badly.
- Publish limit per server is 600 + 240 x players per minute, and subscriptions per server are limited.
- Best effort: no guaranteed delivery or ordering, typically 1-2 s latency, and messages can be dropped, so the list goes stale or flickers. There is no history, so a new server sees nothing until the next broadcasts arrive. Sender clocks differ.
- It is not a database.
Better: each server writes its own small entry to a MemoryStore SortedMap (key = JobId, expiration ~30 s, refreshed every 15-30 s). The lobby reads it with GetRangeAsync (paginated), and the entries expire when a server dies. Use MessagingService only for small "go look" or join notifications.
D17:
Limits: HttpService allows 500 requests per minute per server, across all endpoints. Joins x3 plus per-kill calls blow past that on busy servers, giving HTTP 429 or "Number of requests exceeded limit" errors. External endpoints can also rate-limit you. Http requests must be enabled (HttpEnabled), and the call fails with no pcall.
Correct setup:
- Batch the analytics: queue events in memory and flush one request every 10-30 s (plus on BindToClose), with a token bucket staying under about 360/min. Or use AnalyticsService for game analytics.
- Wrap RequestAsync in pcall. Retry only on 408, 425, 429 or 5xx, with exponential backoff and Retry-After.
- Never hard-code API keys. A key in a script is visible to anyone with edit or place access, and leaks if the place is copied or uncopylocked. Store it with Secrets (Game Settings > Security > Secrets, restricted to the API's domain) and read it via HttpService:GetSecret(name), which returns a Secret you can only use in headers, or AddPrefix. Use local secrets in Studio.
- Give Open Cloud keys minimal scopes, restrict them to the experience and IPs, and rotate the key that was exposed in the script now. Prefer engine services (DataStore, MessagingService) over calling Open Cloud from inside the game.
D18:
Client camera: use RunService:BindToRenderStep("CamFollow", Enum.RenderPriority.Camera.Value + 1, fn) (or RenderStepped/PreRender). These run before the frame is rendered, after input. Heartbeat runs after physics, out of sync with the render, so the camera uses a character position from a different step than the one drawn, and it jitters. Binding after the Camera priority also runs after the default camera script, so neither overwrites the other. Use dt for smoothing.
Server projectile: RenderStepped and BindToRenderStep exist only on clients, because the server has no renderer, so it errors. On the server use RunService.Heartbeat (after physics, receives dt) or PreSimulation/Stepped (before physics) to step projectiles, scaling movement by dt. With 2026 fixed simulation or Server Authority, use RunService:BindToSimulation for deterministic fixed-rate steps. In general, client visuals go on PreRender and game logic on Heartbeat/PreSimulation.
D19:
Use the Input Action System (IAS) for a new 2026 game. It is cross-platform, data-driven, and is the direction Roblox's own player scripts are taking. ContextActionService still works but is legacy and client-only.
Structure: an InputContext (a group of actions you enable or disable and prioritise, e.g. "Gameplay" or "Menu") contains InputActions (Sprint: Type Bool; Interact: Bool; with Direction1D/2D/3D/ViewportPosition types available). Each action contains InputBindings (KeyCode such as LeftShift or ButtonL3, with modifiers and Scale, or a touch UI button). Read action.Pressed, Released, StateChanged or GetState(). The instances can be authored in Studio and exist on both client and server. Bind every action for keyboard, gamepad and touch. Swap contexts instead of sinking input.
Player scripts: the default PlayerModule movement and camera are being migrated to IAS. June 2026: opt-in via Workspace.PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem. Early 2027 (planned): enabled by default. Mid 2027 (planned): the property is removed and the old scripts are gone. Code that does require(PlayerModule):GetControls() or relies on the old CAS sinking will break. Disable the IAS context instead, and forked player scripts need updating.
D20:
Turn it on with Workspace.AuthorityMode = Server (fully released July 2026). This forces NextGenerationReplication, PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem, SignalBehavior = Deferred, StreamingEnabled and UseFixedSimulation.
What it does: the server is authoritative over the simulation, including player characters. Clients no longer own physics; they predict locally and are rolled back and resimulated when the server disagrees. That removes the classic network-ownership exploits (teleport, fling, speed) and gives fair hit results for competitive play.
Script changes:
- Put movement and gameplay simulation in RunService:BindToSimulation(fn, frequency, priority) callbacks, which run on client and server and re-run during resimulation. Guard side effects (VFX, sounds, remotes) with RunService:IsResimulating().
- Read input through the Input Action System (InputAction state), not UserInputService.InputBegan, so the server sees the same input.
- Use time(), not tick() or os.clock(). Use Player:GetCameraState() for the camera.
- Inside bound functions, Destroy, reparenting and EquipTool error. Only the first 64 attributes replicate, with names and values up to 50 characters.
- The game must work with streaming and deferred signals. SetNetworkOwner hacks are not a substitute, so remove them. Don't use remotes as property fences.
- The server still validates damage and purchases.
D21:
API: RunService:BindToSimulation(callback, frequency, priority) (frequency is Enum.StepFrequency Hz60/30/15/10/5/1, default Hz30, priority default 2000). It runs your callback at a fixed simulation rate with a fixed dt on both client and server, independent of render FPS, so 30 and 144 FPS players step identically and match the server. BindToAnimation is the fixed-rate counterpart for animation work.
Requirements: Workspace.UseFixedSimulation must be enabled (Server Authority, AuthorityMode = Server, forces it on). The callback can be re-run during resimulation and rollback, so it must be deterministic: use only the passed dt and time(), no os.clock or tick, and read input from Input Action System state. Guard side effects with RunService:IsResimulating(). Don't do structural changes (Destroy, reparent) inside it. Move the logic out of PreSimulation, whose variable dt caused the mismatch.
D22:
Lighting.Technology is deprecated (2026). It was replaced by two properties: Lighting.LightingStyle (Realistic or Soft) and Lighting.PrioritizeLightingQuality (bool, default true). Technology is now hidden from the Properties window and its script security is restricted (RobloxScriptSecurity), so reading or writing it from a LocalScript or any game script errors. It could never be changed at runtime from a client anyway.
Fix: set LightingStyle and PrioritizeLightingQuality in Studio for the place (Realistic + true is roughly the old Future look). For a quality setting players can change, don't change lighting technology. Toggle client-side extras instead (shadows on lights, post-effects, Atmosphere, particle density), and let the player's graphics quality level handle the rest.

Yes. Instance:QueryDescendants(selector) (2026) takes a CSS-like selector that combines class, tag (.Tag), attribute ([$Attr = value]) and :has/:not, and returns a table:
```lua
local coins = workspace:QueryDescendants("BasePart.Coin[$Collected = false]")
for _, coin in coins do
    -- ...

```
For a live set that updates itself, use CollectionService:CreateCollection("BasePart.Coin[$Collected = false]", workspace), which uses the same grammar. Before this, the efficient way was CollectionService:GetTagged("Coin") filtered by coin:IsA("BasePart") and coin:GetAttribute("Collected") == false, which is still far cheaper than GetDescendants every round.
D24:
All four have built-ins now:
- lerp: math.lerp(a, b, t)
- remap: math.map(x, inMin, inMax, outMin, outMax) (does not clamp, so add math.clamp if you need it)
- NaN check: math.isnan(x) (with math.isinf and math.isfinite)
- bit packing: buffer.writebits(b, bitOffset, bitCount, value) and buffer.readbits(b, bitOffset, bitCount), with bitCount 0-32 and the offset in bits, not bytes. These replace manual shifting with bit32 when packing 3-bit and 5-bit fields into a buffer.
Note: readbits and writebits take a bit offset while the other buffer functions take byte offsets, and out-of-range access throws.
